tlIntro: Every date in one place. Each entry says whether the date comes from the book, from public records, or from both. Entries marked “From the story” were written for the story and have no record behind them.

tlImage.alt: A hand-coloured sketch map of Sydney Cove in 1788. Eleven ships are anchored in the cove. Tents, huts, the Governor’s house and a farm are drawn on the land, with a list of references at the lower left.
tlImage.cap: Sketch and description of the settlement at Sydney Cove, Port Jackson, said to be taken by a transported convict on 16 April 1788. Published in London in 1789.
tlImage.credit: Francis Fowkes (attributed). State Library of New South Wales. Via Wikimedia Commons. Public domain. The book also uses this sketch on its page 2.

events.t: The First Fleet reaches Botany Bay
events.x: The Supply arrived on 18 January 1788, the transports on 19 January and the Sirius on 20 January. The book’s introduction begins with the arrival of the First Fleet in 1788.

events.t: The colony is set up at Sydney Cove
events.x: Botany Bay was judged unsuitable. Governor Phillip arrived at Sydney Cove on the Supply on 26 January, and the Sirius the next day. The book’s plate on page 2 calls the harbour Warrane.

events.t: Sketch of the settlement at Sydney Cove
events.x: The sketch on the book’s page 2 says it was taken on this date. It was published in London on 24 July 1789.

events.t: Smallpox among First Nations people around Sydney
events.x: The National Museum says up to 70 per cent of First Nations people in the area died. How the disease arrived is debated. Most colonists had met it in childhood. The Resistor’s page says a “great sickness” in 1789 devastated the clans.

events.t: Bennelong and Colebee are seized at Manly Cove
events.x: Governor Phillip ordered two men to be captured. Colebee escaped soon after, and Bennelong in May 1790. In Freeman’s story he talks about Bennelong, “a real man with a complicated life”.

events.t: The Sirius sails to Norfolk Island
events.x: She carried Major Ross, a large detachment of marines and more than 200 convicts. Tench says it was hoped that splitting the numbers would help the colony feed itself.

events.t: The Sirius is wrecked at Norfolk Island
events.x: Freeman’s chapter says she was wrecked “earlier this year”. Sirius sources give 19 March 1790. Tench’s printed text says “the 19th of February”, so the date needs checking in the original.

events.t: The ration is cut, from 1 April
events.x: Everyone in the settlement was to get 4 lb of flour, 2½ lb of salt pork and 1½ lb of rice a week.

events.t: A smaller ration begins
events.x: After news of the wreck: 2½ lb of flour, 2 lb of pork and 2 lb of rice (or a quart of peas) a week. The book’s plate on page 38 is dated 12 April 1790 and is labelled a reconstruction, not an original.

events.t: The Governor’s gamekeeper is speared
events.x: Tench wrote that a shooting party went out on 9 December and that McEntire was speared about one o’clock in the night. The National Museum gives 10 December. The book’s plates on pages 19 and 20 are dated December 1790, but Freeman’s chapter says “Last December”.

events.t: Tench marches to Botany Bay
events.x: The order was to bring in six men or, if that failed, to put six to death and bring back their heads. Tench asked for the plan to be changed from killing ten men to capturing six. His party found none of the men Phillip wanted. The book’s Freeman chapter says he must march with Tench “tomorrow”.

events.t: Tench’s second march
events.x: A second, smaller party marched at sunset. It found the huts empty and saw no one. Tench called it a “fruitless peregrination”.

events.t: The first raid at Prospect
events.x: The National Museum says the raids led by Pemulwuy began in 1792 and the first was at Prospect in May. The Bidjigal burnt huts, took maize and attacked travellers. The Resistor’s page opens with a night raid on the Prospect cornfields, with no date given.

events.t: Fighting on the farms is frequent
events.x: The National Museum says that by April 1794 violence between First Nations people and farmers was frequent and widespread.

events.t: Raid at Toongabbie and the clash at Parramatta
events.x: He led a raid on the government farm at Toongabbie. Settlers and soldiers followed his group to Parramatta, where at least five First Nations men were killed. He was wounded by seven pieces of buckshot, was taken to hospital and escaped with an iron on his leg. By late April he was seen near Botany Bay, recovered.

events.t: Orders to shoot on sight, and a reward
events.x: Governor King ordered that First Nations people near Parramatta, the Georges River and Prospect could be shot on sight. In November he outlawed Pemulwuy and offered rewards for his capture or death.

events.t: Pemulwuy is shot dead
events.x: The National Museum says it is not certain who shot him. A later dispatch from London said that cruelty toward First Nations people would be punished.

events.t: Workers break threshing machines in Hampshire
events.x: More than seventy towns and villages were affected. On 20 November a crowd destroyed a factory at Upper Clatford, near Andover. Curtis’s page names the threshing machines as one cause of his ruin.

events.t: The Poor Law Amendment Act
events.x: It ended outdoor relief for able-bodied people. Help was often given only inside a workhouse. The book names “the New Poor Law of 1834”.

events.t: Governor Bourke’s proclamation
events.x: The Australian Museum says this proclamation put the legal principle of terra nullius into Australian law, 47 years after the First Fleet. The book’s Resistor page says the strangers claimed the land by terra nullius in 1788.

events.t: Severe drought in New South Wales
events.x: The Reserve Bank of Australia says the drought forced the colony to import wheat. Curtis’s page puts the drought in the years up to 1842.

events.t: The Andromache sails from London
events.x: The barque Andromache, Captain Thomas New, carried assisted immigrants. The shipping list says the passage took 113 days.

events.t: The Andromache reaches Port Phillip
events.x: The book says Curtis’s ship made “a brief stop at Port Phillip”.

events.t: Eleven passengers go on to Sydney
events.x: They left Port Phillip on 29 July and arrived in Sydney on 2 August. The list includes a Curtis family of four. The book says Curtis arrived “in August 1840”.

events.t: Curtis and Robert are lost and meet Warra
events.x: The book says that by 1842 the river had shrunk to muddy pools. “This evening”, Curtis and Robert go west to look for better land and get lost. This scene was written for the story. The Reserve Bank of Australia places the severe drought in 1838 to 1840.

events.t: Andover bone crushing is raised in Parliament
events.x: A member told the Commons that people in the Andover workhouse fought over the marrow and meat on the bones they crushed. A Select Committee heard evidence in 1846. The book has villagers talking about Andover before Curtis sails in 1840.

events.t: The High Court decides Mabo (No. 2)
events.x: The High Court overturned terra nullius and recognised native title. The book’s Resistor page uses the words “terra nullius”.

events.d: No date given in the book
events.t: Freeman is told to march with Tench “tomorrow”
events.x: The book gives no date. The context of the spearing and the march fits December 1790. No record shows a clerk on the march.

events.d: No date given in the book
events.t: The night raid on the Prospect cornfields
events.x: The Resistor and fifty warriors wait to attack the cornfields at Prospect. Freeman watches from a rise. No record was found of this meeting. The records give the first raid at Prospect as May 1792.
